lessonRef.title: Investigation or close reading: selecting strong work

studentTask.text: This Grade 5 lesson develops selecting strong work within the unit “Publication and Communication Capstone.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's investigation or close reading work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
[1] Near the end of the “Publication and Communication Capstone” workshop at the end-of-year exhibition, Amara reviewed a proposal with a margin full of questions. The first portfolio note claimed, “My final piece is better because I worked harder.” The claim may have been sincere, but it gave a reader no visible way to inspect the growth.

[2] Mateo suggested comparing one paragraph from each version. The early paragraph listed three facts without showing their relationship. The later paragraph grouped two facts as evidence, explained the connection, and set aside the third because it did not support the controlling idea. The change was specific enough to discuss.

[3] A second comparison revealed a tradeoff. The later opening was clearer, but it had lost an image that gave the earlier draft energy. Rather than calling every revision an improvement, Amara restored the image in a new position and recorded why clarity and voice both mattered for the intended audience.

[4] The reflection used selecting strong work to turn a vague statement of pride into an evidence-based account. It named a change, located proof in the work, and explained the decision behind it. It also named a next step, because publication marked the best current version rather than the end of learning.

[5] Before revising, the group tested the source against the workshop goal: selecting strong work. They highlighted language that supported the goal, circled a detail that complicated it, and drew an arrow where the relationship between two ideas needed to be made explicit. The marks produced different possible readings, so the group had to defend priorities rather than copy a single approved answer.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Reading Lab 169: selecting strong work”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what selecting strong work asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Reading Lab 169: selecting strong work,” then answer: Read the source without interruption, then decide which detail most changes an interpretation of selecting strong work. Explain the change.

Deliverable: Grade 5: an evidence log and a short interpretation; write one developed paragraph.

Evidence requirement: Use two quoted or paraphrased details with paragraph numbers. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If selecting strong work is not yet secure, return to “Reading Lab 169: selecting strong work” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply selecting strong work to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Reading Lab 169: selecting strong work.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
